name: Inspect overhead and underground plant
summary: Inspectors work through the utility's poles, pad-mounted transformers, switchgear and vaults on a fixed multi-year cycle, looking for rot, leaning poles, broken hardware, oil leaks, damaged or open enclosures and hot connections, and a share of poles get a strength test each year. Each asset gets a record on a tablet with photos and a priority; urgent hazards go straight to the control room for a line crew, and other deficiencies are reviewed weekly by the field services supervisor and turned into maintenance work orders, tree trimming requests or record corrections. The work is high volume and repetitive, so the slow parts are getting to every asset in the cycle (back-lot poles, locked yards, snow) and the weekly batch review of findings, and the common errors are wrong asset numbers and inconsistent priorities.

baseline.org_archetype: A city-owned Ontario electricity distributor with about 350,000 customers, 49,000 poles and about 39,000 to 47,000 distribution transformers over 1,116 km2.
baseline.notes: Reference period 2019-2022. Inspection routes come from the GIS and ERP; inspectors use tablets with a mobile workforce application that syncs to the ERP; records support the Distribution System Code inspection requirements and the annual Ontario Regulation 22/04 compliance audit.

unit_of_work: one asset inspected (a pole with its overhead equipment, or one ground-level unit such as a pad-mounted transformer, switchgear or vault)
trigger: The asset's area comes due in the multi-year inspection plan and its inspection work order is released.
end_state: The inspection record is in the ERP and GIS, and any deficiency has been made safe or passed on as a maintenance work order, a trimming request or a record correction.

volume.seasonality: Pole testing and back-lot patrols run mostly April to November; ground-level units buried in snow and frozen ground slow work in January and February, when inspectors concentrate on accessible overhead patrols.

evidence.note: About 38,946 transformers inspected regularly and 49,000 poles tested at 10-year intervals (ho_grids2024); routine inspection on a three-year cycle across the territory (ho_grid2024). Estimate per year: 16,300 pole visual inspections (49,000 / 3), 4,900 pole tests, about 8,300 ground-level transformers (about 25,000 pad-mounted / 3) and about 1,000 switchgear and vaults: about 30,500 a year or 2,500 a month. The organisation file's mode of 1,800 implies a longer cycle than the sources state.

Organisation file role and cost (2019-2022 wage x 1.40 for benefits, OMERS pension, payroll taxes and overhead). Eight field service representatives who also do disconnections, reconnections and service checks; this process needs about 5 to 5.5 FTE of inspection at the volume above, more than half of the group.
Organisation file role and cost (2019-2022 wage x 1.40 for benefits, OMERS pension, payroll taxes and overhead). Two supervisors; assign packages, weekly deficiency review and quality sampling.

Organisation file role and cost (2019-2022 wage x 1.40 for benefits, OMERS pension, payroll taxes and overhead). Journeyperson line trades make urgent hazards safe and verify the scope of unclear deficiencies; steps show two-person crews (people = 2).

Organisation file role and cost (2019-2022 wage x 1.40 for benefits, OMERS pension, payroll taxes and overhead). Not in the process map's roles; logs hazard calls from inspectors and dispatches a crew.

systems.name: Mobile workforce management and field tablets
ERP: general ledger, work orders, purchasing, inventory, fixed assets
Geographic information system (asset and network model)
Asset condition and health index analytics
Document management and engineering drawing repository

resources.name: Light vehicle (pickup or van) for locators, meter technicians, inspectors and field service

steps.name: Release the area's inspection orders
steps.description: At the start of the year the ERP generates inspection work orders for every asset in the areas due under the multi-year plan, and they are released to the field services backlog area by area through the year.

evidence.note: Inspection cycles from the sources; the OEB Distribution System Code Appendix C minimum cycles were not opened (its PDF did not render).

steps.name: Assign inspection packages
steps.description: The field services supervisor groups orders into packages of a few hundred assets by area and type, assigns them to inspectors with a due date and pushes them to the tablets; the minutes shown are one asset's share of that work.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Review route and asset history
steps.description: The inspector opens the package map on the tablet, checks the previous inspection result and open deficiencies for each asset and plans a driving route for the day.

evidence.note: Packages are worked over two to four weeks between other field orders.

steps.name: Drive or walk to the asset
steps.description: The inspector drives along the line or between subdivision pad-mounts, parks and walks to the asset, including back-lot poles reached through yards.

next.condition: no access (locked gate, dog, owner refuses)

evidence.note: Author's estimate; shares follow the volume split.

steps.name: Inspect the pole and overhead equipment
steps.description: The inspector checks the pole for lean, rot, woodpecker and vehicle damage, then looks up at crossarms, insulators, transformer, arresters, guys and anchors, conductors and clearances, and tree contact, using binoculars.

error.defect_description: A defect is missed or a defect is rated lower than it should be.

next.condition: infrared scan due on this route

evidence.note: What is checked is common practice; time per pole (about 100 to 150 poles a day on a visual patrol) is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Open and inspect a ground-level unit
steps.description: The inspector checks that the pad-mounted transformer, switchgear or vault is locked and intact, opens it where the procedure allows, looks for oil leaks, corrosion, damaged elbows and animal entry, checks the pad and clearances around doors, and relocks it.

error.defect_description: Enclosure left unlatched or a defect missed.

control.basis: Approach distances and procedure for opening energized pad-mounted equipment (IHSA Electrical Utility Safety Rules)

evidence.note: Regular transformer inspections from the source; steps and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Test the pole's strength
steps.description: The inspector sounds the pole with a hammer, bores or uses a resistance drill at ground line, measures circumference and remaining shell, and records whether the pole passes, needs reinforcement or must be replaced.

error.defect_description: Internal rot missed or remaining strength misjudged.

evidence.note: 10-year pole test interval and critical pole program from the sources; method and time are the author's estimate; testing waits out frozen ground.

steps.name: Arrange access and come back
steps.description: When a back-lot pole or a unit in a fenced yard cannot be reached, the inspector leaves a card or phones the owner, and returns on an agreed day or when the obstacle is gone.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Scan with an infrared camera
steps.description: On infrared routes the inspector scans connectors, transformer bushings, cutouts and switches with a thermal camera while the line is loaded and records any connection hotter than its neighbours.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the result on the tablet
steps.description: The inspector confirms the asset number against the tag, ticks the checklist, attaches photos, and for each deficiency picks a code and a priority (urgent, within 30 days, within a year, monitor).

error.defect_description: Wrong asset number, wrong deficiency code or inconsistent priority.

control.basis: Inspection records kept under the Distribution System Code inspection requirements and Ontario Regulation 22/04

evidence.note: Deficiency rate is the author's estimate for an aging system.

steps.name: Sync the record to the ERP and GIS
steps.description: When the tablet next connects, the mobile workforce application posts the inspection result to the ERP work order and the GIS asset, and the order closes automatically if there is no deficiency.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Report the hazard and stand by
steps.description: For a broken pole, a low or damaged conductor, an open or damaged pad-mount, or a tree on a line, the inspector phones the dispatcher with the location and asset number and stays to keep the public away until a crew arrives.

control.basis: Public safety hazards guarded until made safe (utility public safety policy under Ontario Regulation 22/04)

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Create a trouble order and dispatch a crew
steps.description: The dispatcher enters the hazard as a trouble order in the outage management system, chooses the nearest available crew or trouble truck and phones them the details.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Make the hazard safe
steps.description: A two-person line crew drives to the site, secures or temporarily supports the pole, closes or replaces the enclosure lock, or cuts the line clear, and passes permanent repair back as a work order.

control.basis: Pre-job hazard assessment and approach distances (IHSA Electrical Utility Safety Rules)

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Review deficiencies weekly
steps.description: Each week the field services supervisor exports the new deficiencies, looks at photos, corrects codes and priorities, removes duplicates of open work orders, and decides where each one goes.

control.basis: Supervisor review of inspection priorities (maintenance policy)

next.condition: scope unclear; needs a line trade's view
record error or third-party attachment problem

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Line trade confirms the repair scope
steps.description: A journeyperson line trade reviews the photos, and visits the site when photos are not enough, to say what repair, materials and equipment are needed and whether an outage is required.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Create the maintenance work order
steps.description: The supervisor creates a corrective maintenance work order in the ERP with the asset, priority, description and photos and sends it to work planning for scheduling.

error.defect_description: Order raised against the wrong asset or with too little description.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the inspection system did not create orders automatically in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Pass the tree finding to vegetation management
steps.description: For tree contact or vegetation encroachment, the supervisor emails the finding with the span, photos and priority to the vegetation coordinator for an urgent or cycle trim.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Send a record correction or attacher notice
steps.description: When the asset in the field does not match the GIS (wrong size, wrong location, missing unit), the supervisor sends a correction request to the records group; for sagging or non-standard telecom attachments, a notice goes to the attacher.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Correct the GIS record
steps.description: A GIS technician checks the as-built drawings, updates the asset's attributes or location in the GIS and closes the correction request.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Post findings to condition data and compliance tally
steps.description: The ERP links the deficiency to the asset and the asset condition data, and the inspection counts roll into the cycle compliance tally used for the annual regulatory audit and the asset condition assessment.

evidence.note: Annual compliance audit under Ontario Regulation 22/04 section 13 from the source; the tally mechanism is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Re-inspect a quality sample
steps.description: The supervisor re-inspects a small random sample of completed assets in the field and compares the result with the inspector's record; disagreements are discussed with the inspector and the asset is re-inspected.

control.basis: Annual audit of distributor compliance under Ontario Regulation 22/04 section 13

evidence.note: Audit duty from the source; sampling rate is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Urgent hazard
exceptions.description: A broken pole, low wire, open pad-mount or tree on a line is guarded and made safe the same day before the permanent repair is planned.

exceptions.name: No access
exceptions.description: Back-lot poles and fenced units need the owner's cooperation, which adds days to weeks.

exceptions.name: Record mismatch
exceptions.description: The asset in the field does not match the GIS and the record is corrected.

evidence.note: Stated in a 2024 source; assumed to apply in 2019-2022.

benchmarks.population: Hydro Ottawa transformers, switches and breakers

evidence.note: Stated in a 2024 source; assumed to apply in 2019-2022.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from release of the asset's package to record closed or deficiency referred

evidence.note: Packages of a few hundred assets are worked over two to four weeks and deficiencies reviewed weekly. Not measured.

pain_points.description: Deficiencies wait for a weekly batch review and are re-typed as ERP work orders, so a 30-day priority can lose a week before planning sees it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Back-lot poles and fenced or snow-covered units are hard to reach, which delays completing each year's share of the cycle.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Different inspectors rate the same defect differently, so supervisors re-code priorities and re-inspect samples.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: An in-depth look at Hydro Ottawa's grid maintenance
sources.supports: Routine inspections of transformers, switches and breakers follow a three-year cycle across the service territory; a critical pole program tests thousands of poles a year; maintenance holes are graded A to E; work often needs the area de-energized, which may need a planned outage; vegetation management units are on two- or three-year cycles; satellite imaging twice a year (introduced after the reference period).

sources.title: With great grids comes great reliability
sources.supports: All 49,000 poles are inspected at 10-year intervals; 38,946 transformers are regularly inspected; crews trim more than 60,000 trees in a typical year; customers get 24 to 72 hours notice of planned outages, with letters for outages over six hours.

sources.title: Utilities: Electrical Distribution Safety regulation and technical guidelines
sources.supports: Ontario Regulation 22/04 section 13 requires an annual audit of distributor compliance with sections 4 to 8 and section 14 an annual declaration of compliance; distributors must notify ESA of a serious electrical incident within 48 hours; construction must be inspected and certified safe before use.

assumptions: One case is one asset: a pole with its overhead equipment, or one ground-level unit. Pole-mounted transformers are inspected with their pole.

The 2024 Hydro Ottawa sources (three-year equipment cycle, 10-year pole tests, about 38,946 transformers inspected) are assumed to describe practice in 2019-2022. The OEB Distribution System Code Appendix C table could not be read and is not cited.

Inspections are done by field service representatives, as the organisation file implies. At about 2,500 assets a month they need about 5 to 5.5 FTE, more than half of the eight-person group; many Ontario distributors use dedicated inspectors or contractors for this work.
Infrared scanning of overhead lines is shown on about 12% of pole visits; satellite and remote sensing came after the reference period and are not modelled.
The weather wait on pole testing (s07) has a mode of zero and a long tail for assets that fall due in deep winter.
Urgent hazards are shown as made safe by a two-person line crew with a bucket truck; permanent repairs are separate work orders in other processes.
